pilgrims: Derisive term for European company agents in Africa, in the book
pilot-house: Small enclosed cabin on a steamboat where the helmsman steers
stern-wheel: Paddle wheel mounted at the back of a riverboat
hames: Curved wooden pieces of a horse's collar harness
stretcher: Canvas bed on poles used to carry the sick or injured
cipher: A secret code, or in the book, a worthless nonentity
fossil: Old-fashioned, outdated person, figuratively in the book
tin-pot: Cheap, pretentious, and worthless, as an official or leader
chaps: Informal term for men or fellows, common in British speech
savages: Colonial-era term for African people, used here with prejudice
helmsman: The person who steers a ship or boat
fireman: Crew member who fed coal into a steamboat's boiler fires
custom-house: Government office where import duties on goods are collected
trading-post: Remote store where goods were exchanged with local people
wood-cutters: Workers who cut timber to fuel steamboats along the river
phantom: Ghostly apparition or something unreal and haunting
askew: Crooked, twisted, or out of line with something
smash-up: A violent crash or collision, such as a wreck
fusillade: Rapid, continuous burst of gunfire from many weapons
hammock: Hanging bed of canvas or net, slung between two points
staves: Narrow wooden strips that form the sides of a barrel
caravan: Group of travellers and animals journeying together across difficult country
carriers: Porters who carried heavy loads on foot for expeditions
beads: Small glass trade ornaments exchanged for goods or favours
parasol: Small umbrella used to shade a person from the sun
cartridges: Packed cases of gunpowder and bullets for firearms
ivory: Elephant tusks, a valuable commodity traded in the book
ivets: Metal bolts or pins that fasten iron plates together
rivets: Metal pins hammered to fasten iron plates together
hippo: Short for hippopotamus, a large river animal of Africa
verily: Archaic word meaning truly or indeed, used for emphasis
intrusted: Old spelling of entrusted, meaning given responsibility for something
fairway: Clear, navigable channel of water for ships to pass through
offing: Part of the sea visible from shore, beyond the nearest waters
astern: Behind a ship, toward its rear or stern
bends: Curves in the river, where its course turns sharply
ceremonies: Formal rites or public rituals performed according to custom
inscrutable: Impossible to read or understand; mysterious and unreadable
incomprehensible: Impossible to understand or make sense of at all
uncongenial: Unpleasant or unsuited to one's nature and temperament
eloquence: Fluent, powerful, and persuasive use of spoken language
pretence: False appearance or pretended claim meant to deceive others
sentiments: Feelings, emotions, or opinions expressed about something
abject: Extremely wretched, miserable, or lowly in condition
wretched: Miserable, unhappy, or pitifully poor in circumstances
bewitched: Enchanted or under a spell, as if controlled by magic
imbecile: Foolish or stupid person, an insulting term in the book
sordid: Dirty, squalid, and morally corrupt in character or motive
languid: Weak and lacking energy or enthusiasm, dreamily listless
emissary: Agent sent on a mission to represent another's interests
philanthropic: Charitable, benevolent, and concerned with improving humanity
lamentable: Deserving regret or pity; deplorably bad or unfortunate
sombre: Dark, gloomy, and serious in mood or appearance
brooding: Deeply dark and gloomy, suggesting threatening or sad thoughts
placid: Calm, peaceful, and undisturbed in manner or surface
tranquil: Quiet, calm, and free from disturbance or agitation
august: Dignified and impressive, commanding respect and admiration
sinister: Threatening, evil, or suggesting harm and wickedness
grotesque: Strangely distorted, ugly, or absurdly unnatural in form
contorted: Twisted or bent out of normal shape, often in pain
appalled: Horrified and deeply shocked by something dreadful
monstrous: Huge in size, or outrageously wicked and frightful
clamour: Loud noise, outcry, or insistent demand from a crowd
uproar: Loud, noisy disturbance or commotion among many people
mournful: Sorrowful, expressing grief or sadness in appearance or sound
pitiless: Showing no mercy or compassion toward others
enigma: Puzzling person or thing that is hard to explain
abject-ish: Miserable and degraded, utterly humbled or low in spirit
erect: Upright and straight, standing firmly without bending
absurd: Ridiculous and unreasonable, plainly lacking sense
dominoes: Small rectangular tiles marked with dots, used in a game
bearers: Men who carried loads or litters over long distances
ruined: Destroyed, damaged beyond repair, or fallen into decay
uttermost: Greatest possible extent or utmost limit of something
bulging: Swollen or stretched outward, as if about to burst
intruders: People who enter a place without permission or right
verandah: Covered outdoor porch running along the front of a house
